reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases / Williams Textbook of Endocrinology
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in CYP27B1, the gene encoding renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase
The enzyme defect prevents conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, so activation rather than intake is the problem
Presents in the first year or two of life with rickets, hypotonia, growth failure, tetany or seizures from hypocalcaemia, and skeletal deformity
Biochemistry shows hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, raised alkaline phosphatase, and secondary hyperparathyroidism
The hallmark is a normal or high 25-hydroxyvitamin D with a characteristically low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, distinguishing it from nutritional deficiency
Unlike vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2, there is no alopecia because the receptor pathway is intact
Treatment is lifelong physiological replacement with the active hormone calcitriol, which bypasses the enzymatic block, with calcium supplementation as needed
reference.pathophysiology: CYP27B1 encodes the renal mitochondrial enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into the biologically active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations abolish this final activation step, so despite adequate substrate the active hormone cannot be produced. Deficient 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D reduces intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, producing hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia, which impair mineralisation of growth-plate cartilage and osteoid, causing rickets and osteomalacia. Hypocalcaemia drives secondary hyperparathyroidism, further increasing renal phosphate loss and bone resorption. Because the enzyme, not the receptor, is defective, providing calcitriol directly restores signalling and corrects the disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Renal osteodystrophy / chronic kidney disease mineral bone disorder
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase
Parathyroid hormone, typically elevated as a secondary response
25-hydroxyvitamin D (normal or high) with 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (characteristically low)
Radiographs of wrists and knees showing rachitic metaphyseal changes
Urinary calcium monitoring during treatment to avoid hypercalciuria
CYP27B1 gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Hypocalcaemic seizures or tetany in an infant
Failure to thrive with progressive skeletal deformity
Hypercalcaemia or hypercalciuria from over-replacement with active vitamin D
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent with lifelong physiological calcitriol replacement, which normalises calcium and heals the rickets; growth and bone health are usually restored, provided treatment is maintained and monitored to avoid toxicity.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as ordinary nutritional deficiency and giving only parent vitamin D, which cannot bypass the enzyme block
Not measuring 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, missing the diagnostic low-active/normal-substrate pattern
Confusing it with type 2 disease, where high-dose therapy and receptor resistance apply
Failing to monitor urinary calcium, allowing hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis on active vitamin D
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
management: Lifelong physiological replacement with active vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol), which bypasses the defective 1-alpha-hydroxylase and restores signalling
Calcium supplementation during initial healing to correct hypocalcaemia and support mineralisation
Manage acute hypocalcaemic tetany or seizures with calcium replacement
Monitor calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and radiographic healing of the rickets to titrate therapy
Surveillance of serum and urinary calcium to avoid hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis from over-treatment
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
Metabolic bone and paediatric specialist referral for ongoing management
